content: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection affects approximately 260 million individuals globally and is responsible for an estimated 900,000 deaths annually. These deaths are primarily due to complications of chronic liver disease, such as cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The regions with the highest prevalence of chronic HBV infection are the Western Pacific and Africa. In 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) on viral hepatitis, which aims to eliminate HBV as a public health threat by 2030. This goal involves reducing the incidence of chronic HBV infection by 90% and its associated mortality by 65%. Chronic HBV infection is more likely to develop when the virus is acquired early in life, making perinatal mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) a significant contributor to the global burden of chronic HBV. Furthermore, individuals who acquire HBV through MTCT are at a higher risk of developing chronic liver disease, including HCC, compared to those who acquire the infection later in life through horizontal transmission. To achieve the WHO’s global hepatitis elimination targets, preventing MTCT of HBV is critical. Since 2009, WHO has recommended the universal administration of timely hepatitis B vaccines to all newborns within 24 hours of birth to prevent MTCT and early childhood transmission. While the birth dose vaccine alone is generally sufficient to prevent MTCT in mothers with low HBV viral replication, 20–30% of women with high viral loads still transmit the virus to their newborns despite timely vaccination. In resource-rich countries, pregnant women are routinely screened for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and, if positive, for hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) to identify high-risk infants. These infants may benefit from hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) in addition to timely birth dose vaccination. However, even with active and passive immunoprophylaxis, a significant proportion of infants born to mothers with very high viral loads—particularly those with serum HBV DNA levels exceeding 200,000 IU/mL—remain at risk of infection. Consequently, in high-income countries, HBV DNA quantification has become a standard part of antenatal HBV testing to identify highly viremic women who may require antiviral therapy during pregnancy to further reduce the risk of MTCT. In contrast, in lowand middle-income countries, additional measures to prevent MTCT, such as maternal antiviral therapy, are rarely implemented. Following antenatal screening for HBsAg, it is essential to quantify serum HBV DNA levels using nucleic acid testing (NAT) to determine which pregnant women require treatment to prevent MTCT. However, access to NAT is severely limited in these settings due to its high cost (ranging from $60 to $200 per assay) and the need for sophisticated laboratory infrastructure and highly skilled personnel. An alternative approach involves the detection of HBeAg using laboratory-based immunoassays, such as enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA), or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) employing lateral flow immunochromatographic assays. These tests are more affordable (ranging from $1 to $30 per assay) and accessible compared to HBV DNA NAT in resource-limited settings. HBeAg testing may serve as a practical alternative to NAT for identifying pregnant women with high viral loads who are at increased risk of transmitting HBV to their infants. The WHO guidelines define high HBV DNA levels as ≥20,000 IU/mL, a threshold used to determine eligibility for antiviral therapy during pregnancy. The performance of HBeAg tests in predicting high HBV DNA levels and the risk of MTCT has been systematically reviewed. The sensitivity and specificity of HBeAg tests vary depending on the type of assay used and the preventive measures implemented. Similarly, the performance of different HBV DNA thresholds in predicting MTCT risk has been evaluated. Post-hoc analyses were conducted to assess the maternal HBV DNA threshold during pregnancy at which the risk of MTCT begins to increase despite infant immunoprophylaxis (timely birth dose vaccination with or without HBIG). Additionally, the performance of HBeAg tests in diagnosing high HBV DNA levels and predicting MTCT risk was analyzed. The findings suggest that HBeAg testing could be a viable alternative to NAT for diagnosing high HBV DNA levels in pregnant women with chronic HBV infection. This approach may help identify women who require antiviral therapy during pregnancy to prevent MTCT, particularly in resource-limited settings where access to NAT is restricted.
